name: The seven brethren and their mother
charge: Refusing to taste swine’s flesh under torture, seven times over, in hope of the resurrection
summary: Seven brothers and their mother were taken and compelled by the king, against the law, to taste swine’s flesh, and were tormented with scourges and whips when they refused. Each chose death rather than transgress the laws of the fathers, and each spoke to the king before he died, of the correction of their own people, of the resurrection, and of the punishment waiting for the persecutor. Their mother saw all seven slain within the space of one day and bore it with good courage, exhorting every one of them in her own language, and she died last of all.
offenseFull: Seven brethren with their mother were taken and compelled by the king, against the law, to taste swine’s flesh, and were tormented with scourges and whips when they would not (2 Maccabees 7:1-2). One of them spoke for the rest: they were ready to die rather than transgress the laws of their fathers. The class asked the question the record puts to us now, why swine’s flesh is all through the church today, when these are the ones who stood stiffly for the law and died for it. It also weighed what that answer costs: you truly cannot desire anything left in this world. We are already captives, with the bills and the fourteen hour days; what is it you are leaving behind? There has to be something better.

The king and they that were with him marvelled at the young man’s courage (2 Maccabees 7:12). They marvel, the class said, because they understand there is a certain spirit in these people, something they know. The brothers answered in turn while they watched what was done to the ones before them. The fourth told the king it is good, being put to death by men, to look for hope from God to be raised up again by him, and that for the persecutor there would be no resurrection to life (2 Maccabees 7:14). The sixth told him not to be deceived without cause, for they suffered these things for themselves, having sinned against their God, but that he who strives against God should not think to escape unpunished (2 Maccabees 7:18-19).

The mother was marvellous above all, and worthy of honourable memory, for she saw her seven sons slain within the space of one day and bore it with good courage because of the hope that she had in the Lord. She exhorted every one of them in her own language, filled with a courageous spirit, and took no credit for them: she neither gave them breath nor life, neither was it she that formed the members of every one of them, but the Creator of the world, who formed the generation of man and found out the beginning of all things, would also of his own mercy give them breath and life again (2 Maccabees 7:20-23). The class reads her as the pattern for a house. Children are to be nurtured in the law (2 Esdras 8:12), and fathers are charged not to provoke them to wrath but to bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4). What she had put in them from childhood is what stood up under the whips.
judgmentFull: The hope is written plainly in their own answers. The King of the world would raise up those who die for his laws to everlasting life (2 Maccabees 7:9). That is the hope Daniel wrote of, that they who sleep in the dust of the earth awake, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting contempt, and that they who turn many to righteousness shine as the stars (Daniel 12:2-3), and the reason a man is told to fear the one able to destroy both soul and body rather than them that kill the body (Matthew 10:28). The class drew the mercy of God out of the other half of the fourth brother’s answer: what kind of mercy would it be if the same people who tormented us received an equal reward in the kingdom? That is not a merciful God, if he allows them to do that to us and then gives them the same portion.

The youngest was offered riches, happiness and the friendship of the king, and the mother was called to counsel him; she bowed herself toward the tyrant, laughed him to scorn, and spoke to her son in her own country language instead, telling him not to fear the tormentor but to take his death as his brethren had (2 Maccabees 7:24-29). Last of all, after the sons, the mother died (2 Maccabees 7:41). Nothing in the account promises that the torments would stop short of death. What it promises is that the One who formed them will form them again, and the record keeps the whole household as one witness to it (Hebrews 11:35-38).

text.text: It came to pass also, that seven brethren with their mother were taken, and compelled by the king against the law to taste swine’s flesh, and were tormented with scourges and whips.
But one of them that spake first said thus, What wouldest thou ask or learn of us? we are ready to die, rather than to transgress the laws of our fathers.
Insomuch that the king, and they that were with him, marvelled at the young man’s courage, for that he nothing regarded the pains.
So when he was ready to die he said thus, It is good, being put to death by men, to look for hope from God to be raised up again by him: as for thee, thou shalt have no resurrection to life.

After him also they brought the sixth, who being ready to die said, Be not deceived without cause: for we suffer these things for ourselves, having sinned against our God: therefore marvellous things are done unto us.
But think not thou, that takest in hand to strive against God, that thou shalt escape unpunished.

But the mother was marvellous above all, and worthy of honourable memory: for when she saw her seven sons slain within the space of one day, she bare it with a good courage, because of the hope that she had in the Lord.
Yea, she exhorted every one of them in her own language, filled with courageous spirits; and stirring up her womanish thoughts with a manly stomach, she said unto them,
I cannot tell how ye came into my womb: for I neither gave you breath nor life, neither was it I that formed the members of every one of you;

But doubtless the Creator of the world, who formed the generation of man, and found out the beginning of all things, will also of his own mercy give you breath and life again, as ye now regard not your own selves for his laws’ sake.
Thou broughtest it up with thy righteousness, and nurturedst it in thy law, and reformedst it with thy judgment.
And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
And when he was at the last gasp, he said, Thou like a fury takest us out of this present life, but the King of the world shall raise us up, who have died for his laws, unto everlasting life.
And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever.
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.

Now Antiochus, thinking himself despised, and suspecting it to be a reproachful speech, whilst the youngest was yet alive, did not only exhort him by words, but also assured him with oaths, that he would make him both a rich and a happy man, if he would turn from the laws of his fathers; and that also he would take him for his friend, and trust him with affairs.
But when the young man would in no case hearken unto him, the king called his mother, and exhorted her that she would counsel the young man to save his life.
And when he had exhorted her with many words, she promised him that she would counsel her son.

But she bowing herself toward him, laughing the cruel tyrant to scorn, spake in her country language on this manner; O my son, have pity upon me that bare thee nine months in my womb, and gave thee such three years, and nourished thee, and brought thee up unto this age, and endured the troubles of education.
I beseech thee, my son, look upon the heaven and the earth, and all that is therein, and consider that God made them of things that were not; and so was mankind made likewise.
Fear not this tormentor, but, being worthy of thy brethren, take thy death that I may receive thee again in mercy with thy brethren.
Last of all after the sons the mother died.
Women received their dead raised to life again: and others were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better resurrection:
And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment:
They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
